utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I'd like to apologise to all for our belated start due to some technical difficulties, which I understand have been resolved. There are several matters before we begin the evidence of the next witness. I would like to address three matters first. First, Mr. Karadzic, with regard to the time available to the accused for cross-examination of Witness KDZ-185, the Chamber advised the parties informally on Thursday last week that a maximum of five hours would be permitted for cross-examination of this witness. The Chamber's assessment that a maximum of five hours is a reasonable time for cross-examination was made on the basis of the criteria we have set out previously, and in particular Mr. Karadzic's own estimate of the time needed for cross-examination, Prosecution's estimate of its time needed for direct examination, the Prosecution's estimate of its time needed for direct examination in addition to the witness's two written statements, as well as the scope and subject matter of the witness's anticipated evidence. And as for the time needed for the next witness, Mr. Mandic, considering the following factors: Number 1, the witness testified for 10 days in Krajisnik case, the Prosecution requested a minimum of eight hours to conduct its direct examination of this witness and the large number of documents of exhibits and its page numbers the Prosecution plans to introduce through this witness, the Chamber is of the view that, in total, 20 hours is a reasonable time for the accused's cross-examination of this particular witness. The last matter I would like to deal with in public session is the scheduling. So as you are aware, the Chamber is constrained by the demands on courtroom spaces of all the trials that are currently ongoing. The Registry is, therefore, responsible for ensuring that all trials can sit in accordance with the needs of the respective Chambers, and we are grateful for their efforts to accommodate our requests. In general, it is this Chamber's preference to sit for morning rather than afternoon sessions. And if possible, when there's a courtroom space available both in the morning and afternoon, our preference is to sit from 9.00 to 3.00 p.m., as we originally planned to do so today. I note that on 15th and 16th July, it would appear that this is the situation, and I would therefore like to advise the parties of our intention to sit from 9.00 to 3.00 on those days, subject to any further changes to be advised. And as for today, given the delay in starting, we'll sit until -- during the first session until 11.00, and the next session being 11.30 to 1.00, and we have one hour lunch break, and we'll sit from 2.00 to 3.30. That said, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Do you have anything to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. As you know, my position, the position of the Defence, was presented by Mr. Robinson, along with my own position, that it is only victims who are entitled to protective measures. However, that's not what I wanted to talk about. I want to talk about time. I'm afraid that the Trial Chamber is not going to get the right impression as far as Sarajevo is concerned. The witnesses we've had so far have shown more what they do not know rather than what they do know. They could not tell the Trial Chamber who was where, and what people were doing, and so on. These are key matters. We now have the opportunity of hearing a witness whose job it was to know who was where, and who was shooting, and what people were doing. Therefore, I believe that five hours is insufficient. And also 40 hours for the next witness is insufficient, because the next witness is a participant, a participant over all of five or six years. He knows what happened before the war and what happened during the war itself. So I kindly ask you to reconsider your decision. May it please not be a definite decision? If there is a chance -- or, rather, if the Trial Chamber views that things are moving smoothly, perhaps I could be given more time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that is the position. The President made that plain when he first spoke about giving limitations on time for cross-examination. It's bound to be flexible because it may well be that at the end of a well-conducted cross-examination, the Trial Chamber is of the view that you genuinely haven't finished all the matters that you need to put, in which case proper consideration would always be given to extending that time. It's going to be reasonably flexible. There can be no guarantees. But these are not figures which are absolutely set in stone from the outset. These are the likely figures to be reconsidered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I was about to use the very phrase that my Brother Morrison used. These figures are not set in stone and they're flexible. And depending on all circumstances, we would be prepared to extend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, it will be the case when you will not have wasted the time given to you. That said, we'll draw the curtain and briefly go into closed session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's go to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You may make yourself comfortable, please. For the public information, we allowed this witness some kinds of protective measures, pursuant to Rule 70, to which the accused has opposed. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, it's now your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wonder if I could ask that 65 ter 90181 be called up, please. And your indulgence. And, of course, not broadcast publicly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in light of the measures that have been granted by this Chamber, I will be addressing you by a pseudonym, that being the pseudonym 185. I'll call you Witness 185. So, now, Witness 185, do you see an image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps Madam Registrar [sic] could just give a little bit of guidance on how to operate this microphone to Witness 185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think what matters is not the witness's microphone, but others. So my understanding is that when the voice distortion is also allowed to the witness, the others should turn off their microphone when the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour. And now perhaps I could follow up with my initial question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, the image on the screen in front of you, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. So then would this be able to be the first Prosecution exhibit, filed under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit P1047, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now move into private session, Your Honours, for the next series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you have given statements under oath in relation to matters relevant to the case that brings us here today on two previous occasions, one in the year 2000 and one in the year 2009?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in preparing for your testimony today, have you had an opportunity to review those statements and a number of the documents associated with those statements or referred to in those statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps you can also show them to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask you the question a slightly different way. During our meeting yesterday to prepare for your testimony today, did you have occasion to review those statements that you had given and a number of the documents referred to in those statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This happened yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any changes, corrections, or other additions to make to those statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers as contained in those statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Then, Your Honour, if I could ask that 65 ter 10029, being the statement of 2000, and 22872, being the statement of 2009, be marked as the next exhibits. And there are a number of associated exhibits. I could read those 65 ter numbers out if it assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're going to use -- you're going to put none of them to the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will be putting a small number of the associated exhibits that were mentioned in those statements to the witness today for further amplification, and a small number of additional exhibits, all of which were part of our initial notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit two statements first and then we'll deal with the remainder at the end of the witness's testimony in direct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 10029 will be Exhibit P1048, under seal. And 65 ter 22872 will be Exhibit P1049, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should note that the exhibit number for the pseudonym sheet should have been P1047. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that being under seal as well. Perhaps then we could move into public session and I could read a short summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of the witness's written evidence. This witness, KDZ-185, was in Sarajevo in 1993. He observed shelling against the civilian population of the city. The daily average of shells impacting in the city during his first three months was approximately 1.200. Some of the shelling was random and did not appear to target military objects. Shelling of civilian populated areas was not always heavy, but consisted of one or two random rounds. The witness concluded that this was intended to maintain a feeling of terror. The witness concludes that some shelling was in retaliation for events elsewhere. On 21 March 1993, approximately 2.400 shells were fired, including 400 on the old town of Sarajevo alone. The retaliatory bombardment was preceded by a Bosnian Army attack on the Pale road Serb supply line. The witness also recalls the shelling of a football match in Dobrinja on 1 June 1993. A crater analysis determined the shells were probably fired by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps from Lukavica Barracks. The witness also saw that civilians were targeted by Serb snipers. Around Sarajevo, civilians erected make-shift protection barriers at junctions particularly exposed to sniping. The witness recalls that the airport runway was the only passage in and out of Sarajevo and was used to bring in personnel or equipment, as well as by persons trying to escape. Bosnian Serb forces shot indiscriminately at people running across the runway at night. A third of those killed or wounded were women, children, and the elderly. The witness states that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps enjoyed superiority in weaponry around Sarajevo. Sarajevo Romanija Corps gun positions around Sarajevo were lightly guarded, had fixed positions, and stored ammunitions immediately next to the battery. The witness concluded that General Galic exercised effective control over his forces, including snipers. He based this on, among other things, the fact that Galic could effectively implement cease-fires and the integrated wire communication system he observed at Sarajevo Romanija Corps artillery positions around the city. Protests were made to General Galic about the Bosnian Serbs' shelling and sniping of civilians in writing, in person, and through the media. And that is the summary of the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could now please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are now in private session, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, the first question I'd like to ask you is: Upon your arrival in the city of Sarajevo, did you make any observations as to the safety and security situation in and around the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo (redacted), I believe that the city was under siege (redacted), and the city was cut off from the rest of the world, apart from a road -- military convoys that were managed by UNHCR as well as other international humanitarian organisations, as well as the area that was under the supervision of UNPROFOR on Sarajevo Airport. And this siege was staged by the Serbian Army, and the objective was to cut off the town and to make sure that it could not obtain any supplies, and therefore this would allow them to put pressure on the Bosnian government and to surrender. The city, especially at night, seemed to be completely dead, given that there was rarely any electricity, as it was one of the means of pressure, namely, to cut off electricity. This means that the city could not be supplied with electricity as well as with heating, for using electricity for heating, and it also means that there was no way electric pumps could be used to supply water in the various dwellings in Sarajevo, which means that at night the city was completely dark and seemed to be totally deserted. And there were only fires that one could hear here and there, and there were sometimes artillery fire as well. As far as the daylight situation was concerned, the situation was even more dire because we could see the population was trying to survive, and they were moving about trying to find water in the Miljacka River which goes through the center of Sarajevo or they were using wells that were still operating. They were also trying to look for supplies in supplies centres that were set up in the city thanks to humanitarian aid. The inhabitants of Sarajevo were under constant pressure, because depending on the way snipers were operating as well as depending on the direction of artillery fire, they did not know whether they were going to survive much longer because they were one of the prime objectives or targets of fire. This was the situation that I witnessed when I arrived (redacted) (redacted) in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this answer, you've made several points that I'd like to come back to over the course of your testimony today, and I'll do that by dealing with some of the themes you've spoken about one by one, and by referring back to the statements you've given earlier. First, I'd like to go back to a point in your statement of 2000, on page 13, paragraph 3, (redacted) Now, in regard there -- in regard to sniping, you noted in the original document: "I think that it was important for the Serb side to exercise a permanent pressure of terror. They would do sniping, therefore, from a certain number of positions (redacted) Now -- and in the same document, slightly further at page 16, paragraph 8, you extensively described the effect of shelling on the civilian population of Sarajevo, noting: "As the bombardments coming from the Serbs were completely random and," and I'll quote in your language: [Interpretation] "... and on the town they had not any military targets in mind, which means that it nurtured a climate of terror amongst the population." [In English] Now, when you used this word "terror" as you did on two occasions in respect of both shelling and snipping, what did you mean to convey?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would ask that this question and answer be in public session. I don't think that this is identifying the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's drawn specifically referencing a document under seal, Your Honour, and when the question is drawn from that document under seal, I think it's appropriate that the examination -- the question remain in private session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But when you asked the witness to expand on the meaning of "terror," and when we hear the answers from the witness, I don't think there would be any danger of revealing the identity of the witness. So would you agree to go back to open session, ask the last question again, and hear the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do that. We go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in your previous statements, when you used this word "terror" in respect of both shelling and sniping, what did you mean to convey?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this word "terror" applied very well to the situation of civilian populations, because by nature they do not have any weapons and they cannot retaliate. When you are in a situation whereby you find yourself in a situation where at any time you could be severely hurt or killed by a sniper or by a shell that could fall anywhere in the city, this nurtures this feeling of terror. (redacted) (redacted) When you have an experience in that field and when you have weapons that you can use to defend yourself, and you know that your life is at stake, the situation is altogether different compared to the situation of a civilian, when you don't have any weapons to defend yourself. And this is why I believe that in that case you are under a feel of terror.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's one line that I think needs redaction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lines 23 and 24, the answer in that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could give me the reference number of page numbers and para number of the translated English -- from the English translation later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour. If the page numbers differ between the two versions, I'll say that. Otherwise, where I don't say it and only provide one reference number, the page numbers are the same as between the two versions. So I've referred to page 13, paragraph 3, and page 16, paragraph 8, and that's the same in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid we don't have para 8 on page 16. Could you check it later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that case, I apologise, and I certainly will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you perceive any over-arching objective to the shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I believe that all those actions which had for a prime objective to terrorise the civilian population had one single objective. They wanted for the civilian population to give up, from a psychological point of view, and they wanted to make sure that the party taking the siege make the other party give up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure when I said "they," actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just said: "They wanted for the civilian population to give up, from a psychological point of view, and they wanted to make sure that the party," your indulgence for just a moment, "taking the siege would make the other party give up." So when you say "they" in that regard, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I'm referring to those who were holding the siege; namely, the Serbian Army, it goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to move on to another subject, being shelling, and may I move into private session for the next question, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: From the beginning of the siege in Sarajevo, there was a monitoring system that was in place with a UN military observer, and their main mission was to report on shelling activities or fire activities of Serbian and Bosnian forces coming from the city and coming from outside the city. (redacted) had a network of observer that were on the Bosnian side, (redacted) had observation positions called Papa and Presidency, and (redacted) a network for the Serbian side outside of the city with observation post called Lima, like "Lukavica." And those observation posts were reporting on shelling that had been carried out by the one or the other belligerent party, based on information such as the fires, the outcreps, as well as the arrival of shells. And they were called increps. So outcreps and increps. And based on this information, (redacted) a very clear idea as to the shelling activity of the various forces that were at hand.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Based on the reports that we would receive, (redacted) confirmations on information that (redacted) on the various artillery input and heavy weapons that the Serbian forces had, as well as the Bosnian forces had, and (redacted) confirmation that there were quite a lot of heavy weapons owned by the Serbs outside of Sarajevo and this was in support of the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of the type of shelling coming into the city, was there any variation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Well, indeed, yes. From the Serbian side, given that the types of artillery of the Serbian forces, namely, the Republika Srpska, were coming from the former JNA, namely, the Yugoslav Army, they had the typical heavy weaponry, a lot of tanks as well, as well as the -- whereas the Bosnian had an improvised army, if we could say so, because it was created out of nothing, and they had very little heavy weapons. They had mainly infantry units, and they had very little artillery units. (redacted) (redacted) they had a multiple rocket-launcher that they were carrying around the city, but they mainly had mortar shells that they were using as heavy weapons and they did not have any heavy pieces of artillery, unlike the Serbian forces. But I'm talking about Sarajevo itself there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of the manner of shelling into the city, did you see fire -- in terms of the manner of shelling into the city, what types of incoming fire did you see?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I saw two types of artillery shelling. The first type was truly military actions, traditional artillery use just to support a military action. Thus, I saw one of the Serbian Army's actions on -- that put me aside, where there were tanks attacking with shelling. But that was a truly military action, and I would say that this had a military aim. They wanted to win ground. The second type of artillery use was to increase psychological pressure on the population and also on the Bosnian government, so then they were just firing at random on the city in a totally random fashion, and that is something which I had the opportunity to see, since I was stationed in the city. So we were also exposed to these random shellings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could please go into private session to refer to an answer the witness has given in that regard and ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a few moments ago, Witness, you referred to something called outcreps and increps. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: (redacted) the reports from the UN observers, and these were very detailed reports. They detailed the outgoing shellings, and also stating the type of weapons used, MROs and guns and anti-tank weapons and anti-aircraft weapons, so that was the outgoing shelling. And the second category was the ingoing [as interpreted] shelling when they could determine the type of ammunition which was arriving on the targets, when there were such targets. And these two categories of observations were subdivided or specified as coming from the Serbian side or coming from the Bosnian side. This, of course, was in principle, what arrived from the Serbian side was aimed at the Bosnian side, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please ask for 65 ter 09583, a Sector Sarajevo sitrep for the time-period of 20 to 21 March 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, is this one of the -- first of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document, which reads "Daily Sarajevo Shootrep/Increp," is that the "increp/outcrep" report you referred to earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct. You can see first the outcreps, the outgoing fire, and then after that you see the increps, and there is a separation between coming from the Serb side and coming from the Bosnian side and the type of material used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of this page, I note paragraph 4 reads: "The following incoming fire was observed on Bosnian-controlled areas:" And it lists artillery at 1.570; mortar, 532. And if we could go to page 4, please. "Tank, 60," on page 4. And the next question I would like to ask you, then: Does this document and this information relate to any situation you've previously given about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct. If you look at the dates that corresponds to the time when there was a peak of shelling and that I observed myself, and that peak occurred at the moment when there was the attack of a Bosniak brigade to the Serb supply line, and in fact there was then -- on the side of the Serbs, they defended themselves, and they then shelled the city and the Bosniak positions in the city on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this document please be given the next Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be put under seal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just double-check, please, the first page of the document. I don't see a need for it to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that exhibit will be admitted as Exhibit P1050.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, did you see any particular peaks in the shelling during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I just mentioned the preceding case, this peak which followed on an attack by a Bosnian brigade. I did witness certain accompanying actions or accompanying military action, but during the first months I was staying in Sarajevo, I saw that pressure was kept at a high level continuously, and, as I said, the average number of shells was about 1200 on the city, and that really kept a climate of terror. Of course, there were a number of shellings which were purely military and which had military targets and others which had -- which were only aimed at creating the psychological pressure and terror which I already described. Other examples, well, I'm thinking of what I could remember. I know that there have been other cases. When there were visits from authorities from the outside who came to visit us, we had the impression that both parties tried to show that Sarajevo was constantly under fire, that there was a war going on, and they were trying to prove -- well, they were trying to provoke each other without us being aware who was the one who started it, and this led to artillery shelling which was constant whilst the visitors were present in Sarajevo. I remember one day - I think it was the end of January - when the responsible of the UNHCR, Ms. Ogata, was present, and while she was there, there was artillery shelling going on nonstop, which could really give the impression that war was raging, there was a raging war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've just spoken of two peaks in shelling, one in the end of March and one in the end of January, corresponding to different factors. Do you have any other examples of peaks in shelling in that regard?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes. We could also establish a parallel between the negotiations which were ongoing either in New York or in Geneva, and this often led to greater violence in Sarajevo, probably because one party or the other wanted to show that things had to change and that negotiations were needed. I should also like to note that this violence peak which I just referred to at the end of March happened at a moment when the majority of the Bosnian government was absent because I think they were in New York at that point in time, so we still have to see whether the aim was not on the part of the Bosnians to show that they still had resources left and that they wanted to go to negotiation, but this is just speculation on my part. The only ones who know for sure are the authorities concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the time I'm taking, Your Honours, but it is, as you can appreciate it, a sensitive situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: We do appreciate that, Madam. We do appreciate that, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask if we could go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, can you please put your pseudonym, which is KDZ-185, and the date of today, which is 28th of June, 2010, on this map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excellent. Both maps, marked and unmarked, will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The annotated map will be Exhibit P1051, under seal. And the un-annotated map will be Exhibit P1052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do you have to put it under seal, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the marked map, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I respond to you on that after the break, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I note the time. We go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since there's a matter the Chamber discussed with the parties, we suggested starting in the absence of the witness. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies again, Mr. Witness. We had some administrative matters to deal with, so we started a bit late again. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, then, we could deal with -- in open session with the map that we've just concluded with, Your Honour, to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it could be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask, please, if we can have the map that's 65 ter -- pardon me, P1021 brought up on the screen. 65 ter 11789, it formerly was, and it appears at page 24 in the Prosecution's map book.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see an image of a map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall having viewed this map during the course of your interview in 2009 and in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention and everyone's attention to the text box that -- the small text box that appears at the right-hand side of the page, not the ones on the right edge of the screen, but the smaller one before. Yes. And if we could -- we have a translation and an enlargement of that text box available as item 26 in the OTP's map book. I'll come up with the 65 ter number momentarily just to be able to display the translation of that item, Your Honour. The magnification of this is actually quite good. 65 ter 13637. And once we have the item number, I can deal with the questions. Thank you. Now, we see on this map, Sarajevo Romanija Corps map which dates from 1994, in this text box an overview of equipment under control within the 20-kilometre area and outside the 20-kilometre area. And, Your Honours, I would like to ask a question now that refers specifically to a passage from one of the witness's statements given earlier on. May we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now back in open session. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement of the year 2000, page 15 -- e-court page 15, paragraph 4, you refer to weapons held by the warring factions and set out some certain numbers held by the forces around Sarajevo, saying: [Interpretation] "Around Sarajevo, there were some 300 heavy weapons of a calibre above 14.5 millimetres, ranging to 152 millimetres, including MRLs, but most of the weapons were artillery guns, anti-tank guns, or 102-millimetre and 152-millimetre guns." [In English] Now, Witness, do you see any correspondence here in this document between the numbers of weapons held by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the information you gave in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: If I refer back to the chart that is in front of me on the screen, it is dated 1994, and I was not in Sarajevo at the time. But I note that the figures in the 20-kilometre zone roughly match the figures I had in mind when I arrived in Sarajevo early 1993. Of course, there must have been fluctuations in between the dates, but it's roughly in keeping with my estimate. And you can see in the chart that are only mentioned weapons above a calibre above the heavy machine-gun which are of a 14.5-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do we have the year noted in this document? Is it 1994? Where do you have it? Or, Mr. Witness, how did you understand this to be related to 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is what the Prosecutor just said two minutes ago. She said that this was a chart dated 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's following the creation of the total exclusion zone in February 1994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on to another subject, then, Witness, the subject of sniping: In your statement of the year 2000, e-court page 13, paragraph 2, you noted: [Interpretation] "I have never been to sniper nests, but we had information as to the way they had been set up." [In English] Could you explain what that information was that you had as to the way they had been set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn, please, to an incident which took place in Dobrinja on the 1st of June, 1993, which you've referred to in your previous statements, a shelling of a football game. Do you recall that incident, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to attend the scene?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes. Given the high number of losses and the fact that a lot of children had been affected, and I was also available at the time, so I went on-site to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, now for 65 ter 11383, page 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see, Witness, the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A crater analysis report on a mortar attack on Dobrinja, June the 1st at 1020. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, and I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be? Madam Usher, could you scroll down in the document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: It is a report that was made by an (redacted) who went on site in order to look at the crater to see what sort of shells fell, in order to see the direction from which those shells were coming from, and to also determine, if possible, the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could -- if I could ask at this moment for private session, Your Honour. I would like to ask a question of the witness that may relate to his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you look, please, Witness, at the following two pages attached to this crater analysis report, and tell us whether you have any comment on these two pages' diagrams.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: As for the first page, it seems to be accurate regarding the point of impact of the shells that fell in this area, and you can see the general direction of the fire, and so we can deduce from there where was the point where those shells were fires. But there is some margin of error, but we can see that the angle is the south-east, so it was in the direction of the south-east and it was coming from the Republika Srpska -- it was on the side of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if these pages 9, 10, and 11, which form Appendix A to this document, could be admitted, please, only these three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're suggesting tendering only three pages of this document; is that correct ?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 9, 10, and 11. Very well. This is -- yes, we'll admit those three pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on --

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: You asked me to talk about the following two pages, but I've only seen one on the screen so far. There we go, we have the second one. Well, I would have the same comments regarding the second page. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We appreciate your precision, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on to your statement of 2009: In response to questions about documents emanating from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, you said, and I'll quote: [Interpretation] "As far as I'm concerned, this is additional evidence that the Bosnian Serb commander or commanding structure was very centralized and 7 no action on the ground, namely, shelling or sniping, was carried out without an authorisation coming probably from the highest level of the hierarchy." [In English] Do you recall giving this answer?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, of course, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you expand on this answer, please? And perhaps I could guide you with this first question. What exactly about these documents led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: You're talking about the reports that were drafted by General Galic to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Very well. I learned on that occasion, during the 2009 interview, that General Galic, as a highly professional military man, reported to his command every evening about everything that had happened within the SRK, and about the various meetings that he may have had with different persons. He was also talking about the various meetings that he would have had during the day. So this is a proof that the military organisation was working very well. The other point that shows that there was a very good hierarchy, which is what you should have in a professional army, and the reason why it shows that it was working very well is that every time there was negotiations at the airport, as one knows, it was UNPROFOR that was in charge of security. Whether there were delegations, Croatian, or Serbian, in Lukavica or they were coming either from Lukavica or from Kiseljak, I don't quite remember, but we would take charge of the transport from those sites, and there was never any fire against UN convoys that were taking those people to the location where negotiations would take place. And after the negotiations, whatever the time that negotiations would be concluded, whether it was early or very late at night, there was also no problem for those delegations to go back to the location where we had taken charge of them in the first place, so whether it was Lukavica or any other location. And most of those negotiations were organised in order to set up a cease-fire that was more or less long, depending on the will of the various warring parties, and we noticed that when there was a cease-fire that was assigned, the shelling would almost cease immediately to the second as soon as the cease-fire had been agreed upon, which showed that the command system from both sides, actually, was working very well. It also showed that the decision was made at corps level. But I believe that General Galic - and in fact I've seen that in light of reports he drafted - General Galic would not have failed to report to his superiors before taking any initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton and Mr. Robinson, unless there's a serious objection, I would tell the Registry to redact the second part of line 2 of page 57. But I take it the words that appears in line 18 on page 57 would be okay. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you said that -- in your answer -- in your 2009 statement, when you said that shelling and sniping, in particular, would not take place without an authorisation coming from the highest level in the hierarchy, were you referring to specific shelling and sniping incidents, then, individual incidents?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: No, I was talking about this from a general point of view. And as for specific incidents, what was quite telling is that all shelling or all sniping would stop as soon as a cease-fire had been agreed upon. I was actually surprised, myself, because I felt or I thought that snipers were far less controlled than they were. In fact, they were perfectly controlled. And I should like to add something that I forgot to say earlier on, that from a general point of view when talking about the Army of Republika Srpska, as I said, it was derived directly from the Yugoslav Army, and as I was saying, the Republika Srpska had been very based, if I could say, in a culture where there was very little initiative at lower levels in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will conclude my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Then we'll come to your associated exhibits. You're going to tender all of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's actually one I'd like to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it, by any chance, 8191? No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to withdraw 14344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll accept, but for that 14344, all of the associated exhibits will be admitted, and the Court Deputy will assign the number and circulate them in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have about 20 minutes before the second break, Mr. Karadzic. Do you like to begin your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not that I have this burning desire to do so, but it's for the Trial Chamber to decide. Whatever you decide is fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's begin your cross-examination. However, while I understand your dissatisfaction with the protective measures, but bear that in mind, it is much better than hearing entire evidence in the closed session. And then I take it you understood what measures should be taken to ask certain categories of questions, so I would expect your co-operation, and I believe that will save our time as well. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I shall do my best to put brief questions so that yes or no would suffice as an answer. That should help us finish on time. Therefore, I would like to remind you of some parts of your previous statements. Is it correct that when you first came to our town, that most of the damage had been caused at the front-line, was registered at the front-line, itself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I think that according to what I saw, the front-line was rather extensive. If we look at all the damage which had been caused around the airport area, especially, and also around the access to the new town, in the old town it is true that there was less damage, except that the library had been totally destroyed, which was quite significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you do confirm that most of the buildings had been intact, as you had put it once?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I can't really say that most of the buildings were intact. For me, "intact" means that there is no trace whatsoever of shelling or of shooting. Most buildings, and especially modern buildings, bore traces of some fire. There were broken windows, window-panes, which clearly showed that shells had fallen either in the vicinity or on the building itself. But as I said earlier on, since most of the artillery shellings were random, most of the buildings were not completely destroyed; far from that, even. But when you want -- when buildings -- when people wanted to destroy buildings, then other measures were used, if we look at what was published in the newspaper "Oslobodjenje".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: (redacted) If you wish, I can even give a direct quote. The question was: [In English] "You said that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just let's go back -- go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "A. Yes. This is in keeping with my prior statement, when I said that the artillery fire on Sarajevo aimed either at supporting proper military actions on the front-line with major destruction of buildings or at having random shelling, which in that case would not destroyed as much." [Interpretation] Is this what you said, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. I repeat that most buildings were completely destroyed, except for certain targets which had been decided by I don't know whom. I can quote the newspaper, "Oslobodjenje," I can also quote other sources, but most of the other -- most of the total destructions were not far from the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you now: Right now, you added something that you never said before, "totally destroyed." You never said "totally destroyed" before. What was it that led you to say that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Between the term "destroyed" and "totally destroyed," there's not a big difference. For me, it is the case when you can no longer live in a house because -- or dwelling because you have no protection left, when the public utilities are no longer available. But, of course, there's a subtle difference between "totally destroyed" and just "destroyed." I just want to say that it is a stronger way of saying exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about buildings on which the window-panes were broken; are they just damaged, or destroyed, or totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: No, I explained earlier on that they were just -- these were damaged, but some of the modern buildings of the city of Sarajevo bore traces. Either the window-panes were broken, or there had been fires after the impact of shelling, or there were traces of firing. But people were still living in those buildings, fortunately for them. And I would like to add, to be even more precise, that along the front-line, and especially near Dobrinja and close to the airport, this reminded me of things I saw during the siege of Stalingrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which buildings in Sarajevo had been totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes. I already quoted two buildings, the newspaper, "Oslobodjenje," where they only had the underground part where the journalists were working, and I went to see it; the Rainbow Hotel building, which was not far from the place where I was staying, myself, and these buildings were not on the front-line. The library building, well, it was not -- the walls were still standing, but there was nothing much left inside. So this showed that there were clearly-chosen targets for certain reasons. For the Rainbow Hotel, the aim was to get the UN people who were staying there to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am not going to state what the situation was in which you had said this, Witness, but can you confirm what you said; namely, that you were familiar with the situation concerning the 10th Mountain Brigade in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Is that a question? Could you please reformulate your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the 10th Mountain Brigade and its commander, Musan Topalovic, nicknamed Caco?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the various sectors where the various Bosnian brigades were stationed outside Sarajevo, and I knew what the sector of the 10th Mountain Brigade was, of course. I know that for the event we referred to this morning, the 10th Brigade tried to cut off the supply line of the Serbian Army on the road to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that the area of responsibility of the 10th Mountain Brigade that was commanded by Caco was within the town rather than out of town?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Based on the information I had, yes, they were stationed or at least they were on the front-line, as was the case for all Bosnian brigades which were holding the front-line facing the Serb units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned that the objective of their attack was -- or, rather, it was the 21st of that month that you had mentioned -- was to cut off the supply line, what was their ultimate objective? Was it not to take Grbavica, Lukavica, and parts that depend on that supply line ultimately?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I have no idea about that since I was not a member of the Bosnian command who knew what they were doing. The only thing I saw was that there was an attack of the 10th Mountain Brigade on this supply line. The final aim that -- I was never informed of the final aim by the Bosnian military superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wasn't that objective obvious? If the supply line is being cut off, is that not intended to take away what had been cut off?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I'm not here to do any strategic -- strategise. I'm just here to tell you what I experienced personally. I will not say any more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm noting the time. We'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: An hour or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have an hour. We'll resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, I will very, very briefly put to you something that you said on earlier occasions, and if you fail to recall that or I need to quote from somewhere, I'll ask for private session. Until then, that will not be necessary. Do you remember saying, about Caco, that this is not a man you would like to meet often?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, after I met him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he is a well-known criminal, almost like his entire staff?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I knew that he had some issues with the judicial system beforehand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the end, he organised an armed insurgency against the authorities and he was liquidated? You mentioned that he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. That was after I left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that his command was at Bistrik, about 100 metres from the command of the Egyptian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, his headquarters were, if I remember properly, opposite the barracks where the Egyptian Battalion was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say on certain occasions that you were aware that the Bosnian -- that is, the Muslim side wished to keep Sarajevo in the focus of international attention and present it as a very serious situation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say on certain occasions that you had seen at least one multiple rocket-launcher that was mobile and was moved around different parts of the city? In the possession of the Muslim army, of course.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Personally, I did not see this multiple rocket-launcher. I heard it as it fired on several occasions not far from the place where I used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you said on occasion that the Muslim side shot in the back of the UN forces, who were on their way to assist in the repair of power supply lines and other installations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I said so, and I witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall saying that it was in the interests of the Muslim army that power supply lines should not be repaired and that that was the reason for their action, rather than something personal against you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: One moment, please. I didn't quite understand your question. You said between the fact that the Muslim or Bosnian army did not want the power supply lines to be repaired -- and then I failed to understand the second part of your question. Would you mind repeating it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That that was the reason why they shot at you, that they wanted to prevent you from assisting in the repair, not that they had anything personal against you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I understand better now. Yes, I believe that they wanted to prevent the lines from being repaired. And at any rate, as far as I know, they didn't know I was present, they didn't know I was among the repair team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you said that this multiple rocket-launcher was set up in the vicinity of your location so that they would associate their firing position with the UN location and thus stop the Serbs from retaliating or at least have the Serbs take the blame for shooting at the United Nations force?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: No, I do not think so. I will give you some explanations. Indeed, they would use -- or they would get closer to the UN force positions in order to fire, in the hope that the Serbian Army would not fire back at them since they were positioned in the vicinity of UN installations. So as it were, they were seeking shelter behind our very relative humility, because we had wounded and killed among our personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they inform you that before your arrival, General Sidoranko [phoen] had presented such a request to Siber to move closer to the United Nations and fire from there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and I do not know a General Sidoranko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Never mind. We have that document in evidence, so I won't insist. Did you say, although it does follow from your confirmation, that it was in the interests of the Muslim side to dramatise the situation in Sarajevo, especially at times of cease-fire, when the media attention towards Sarajevo was lower, that they would intensify even sniper fire against their own people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I can't remember what I said exactly in those documents, if any, but I can state this now: I do believe that in order to make up for their inferiority, in military terms, the Bosnian government would carry out a kind of media war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for that purpose, they staged various dramatic incidents around the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: That's what I was told, and I believe that I, too, have witnessed such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had one opportunity to eye-witness that a shell targeted a building in Markale, had been fired from Muslim territory, with an error of margin of maximum 300, 400 metres, and it was obvious that the Serbs could not have fired it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I did not witness this, this hit, with my own eyes, but I know it reached the courtyard of a residential block not far from the Markale market-place, and there were crater analyses carried out then which, indeed, showed that it was very likely that the shell was fired from a position close to the front-line to the north of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was that crater analysis done, in which period?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the exact date right now. But as to the analysis, the crater analysis, it was carried out straight away as soon as the UN, the UNPROFOR, heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it of any significance that the analysis was done immediately after the event?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because in this way it could be made sure that there was no meddling with the data on the ground, so that you could have as objective a crater analysis as possible, you couldn't tamper with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the site, itself, deteriorate naturally, without any tampering, unless the analysis is done immediately?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I think that you can remove evidence or traces, for instance, fragments of shells all around, and also the impact of the shell, itself, will fade away with time, as time goes by. So, you know, time does its work, so you have to carry out this type of analysis as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were also protest notes sent to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina over the targeting of a location just 200 metres away from the PTT building, and the Muslim army was warned not to do that again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) I had been in Sarajevo for a while, and I saw that just about every night there were killed and wounded among the civilian population, children, women, elderly people, due to Serbian fire, flanking fire on the airport, using the part where the people were trying to come in and out of Sarajevo, and I thought this was inadmissible, unacceptable. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I'm about certain that I said that, because eventually you realise that if the Sarajevo population was generally hostage to the Serbs, because it was a besieged city within the city, there were other hostages, i.e., the Serbian minority held by the Bosnian Muslim authorities, to start with. And this phenomenon recurred later on in spring, when they also held within the city the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you said the Serbs fired at the runway. Did the Muslims also fire at the runway from Butmir, and did you state so at least on one previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslims from Butmir, as far as I know, never fired on Bistrik. I fail to see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said "runway," not "Bistrik." "Runway."

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Oh. On the landing strip on the runway, there were some stray shells because the airport was in the very heart of the confrontations between the Serbs and the Muslims. Inevitably, there would be shells landing that could land in the airport area when there was crossfire -- when there was an exchange of fire between various parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up -- and I hope we can now move to open session. Can we call up 1D442.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while waiting, Witness, can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you want to go back to open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think we may now. I'll be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you state once that by night, it was not possible to distinguish who was a civilian and who was a soldier among the people who were looking for the runway?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Serbs would have acted differently if they had been able to distinguish between soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I cannot say anything in this regard. All I can say is I saw civilians, children, women, and the elderly in -- that were killed or injured in the area of the runway of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to look at this document now. It's a document from the 10th Mountain Brigade, dated 28th February. This is all you need to see. They notified that on 19 February, between 11.00 and 12.00, an unidentified female person of elderly age was wounded in an attempt to escape to the occupied territory, and in their terminology, "occupied territory" is Grbavica: "Since this is a frequent occurrence and it always happens across the zone held by the HVO, and that all previous attempts were prevented by opening fire and then pulling out the wounded, with danger to the lives of our fighting men, we demand that the necessary action be urgently taken, in terms of security, with HVO units to finally put an end to this." This means that an elderly woman, who was trying to get across to Grbavica, was shot by them. Did you know about such things happening?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I would like to obtain a translation, either in English or in French, of this document, because unfortunately I do not speak Serbo-Croatian and I'm not able to read it, either, whether it's in Latin alphabet or in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is indubitably a document from the 10th Mountain Brigade. It was signed by the assistant commander in charge of security, Senad Hasic [phoen]. This is beyond doubt. It's a document obtained by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a pure waste of time. Just put your question, whether he knows the incident or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that they had held civilians in the city. Are you aware that they were also prepared to shoot at people who were trying to get away without their permission, and they actually did shoot at them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I haven't been made aware of this specific incident. I do know that, indeed, government forces had established control positions in Dobrinja. It's a road that is parallel to the runway, and they were checking people going through towards the airport. So no one could really go without being checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an incident where a person was wounded. It was an attempt to kill a person at Vrbanja Bridge. Do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: And unfortunately, he is notorious in my country for reasons that you know very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I followed your last answer, Mr. Witness. Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, but I can also expand on this. Port Vrbanja was the location where a French position of UNPROFOR was attacked by Serb troops that were wearing UN uniforms, and so this is what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you heard of the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not of the incident that Mr. Karadzic, the accused, was talking about, but I know the bridge, Vrbanja. I knew where it was, and I also went there eventually. I knew very well where it was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, following our principle, we'll not admit this because the witness was not able to confirm anything about this one and knew nothing about the incident, but for the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was more interested in the phenomenon, as such. I know that he couldn't be aware of each and every incident, but it is up to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I said "knew nothing about the incident, but for the bridge." Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, did you say that you escorted a high official of your country to a Serb settlement, on which occasion the Muslims shot at you to stop that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Stop there. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I now remind you that (redacted) (redacted) you stated that you had been aware that the reason for Serb attacks was their wish to prevent the Muslim attack on their supply lines, and you confirmed that today. That's the incident of 21st March.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, the incident on the 21st of March was designed in such a way by Serb forces to wage a counter-attack and to retaliate against the attack from the 10th Mountain Brigade, but their response was of a disproportionate nature because part of the shelling targeted the old town, whereas the soldiers of the 10th Mountain Brigade were actually not based in the old town. They were on the front-line, and in parallel -- we've seen it yesterday because figures were showed by the Prosecutor. We saw, as I was saying, that there was a retaliatory fire organised by Serb forces in the proximity of the airport near Butmir by artillery forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case that the staff and the logistics and the whole base of the 10th Mountain Brigade were in Bistrik, and Bistrik is a part of the old town?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: The General Staff of the 10th Mountain Brigade was opposite -- on the opposite side of the headquarters of the Egyptian Battalion, but it was an area that was rather restricted in surface area and most of the shelling targeted the old town beyond the Miljacka River. So I believe that it was rather surprising to have really pounded the old town while actually trying to target the headquarters of the 10th Mountain Brigade. As for the logistics of the Serb, Bosnian, Muslim brigades, they were of a small nature, because in order to get supply, albeit food or munitions, they didn't really need a logistical depot, and as for fuel, they did not need any, because they were fighting on foot.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: (redacted) how many troops of the 10th Mountain Brigade were in the area where the shells were falling?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: You mean how many soldiers there were in the old town? As far as I'm concerned, I don't think there were many soldiers. The soldiers were on the front-lines, so above the Jewish cemetery on the road to Pale, and they were not fighting based in the old town. They were fighting in the outskirts of the old city when going towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I would like to come back on troop deployment, and I mean troops from the Bosnian government. I experienced this part of the war within the city of Sarajevo, so I know full well what was happening there, unlike others. And I know full well that Bosnian troops were deployed on the front-line. They had no barracks, apart from small headquarters. And when soldiers were taken off the front-line, they were going back home. In fact, they were going back home without their weapons, because there was not enough weapons for everyone, and so I have witnessed columns of soldiers that were going to the front-line and they didn't have weapons because they would swap weapons or exchange weapons when they arrived on the front-line. So the fact that some soldiers were based in the city is actually not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that one organic component of the 10th Mountain Brigade was the Anti-Sabotage Detachment, Bascarsija, from Old Town, and they were deployed all over the old town, their logistics were in different locations? Their staff was small, but their staff units were all around in Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: This is information I never received or obtained. But I was going about the whole of the city of Sarajevo, including the old town,

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: (redacted) I'm quite surprised by what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will present that, but I'm very happy that you know all about Sarajevo, because we were really looking forward to a witness who knows all about what happened in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D1872, please. I believe that there is a translation. Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, now we are slowly moving on to the 1st of June and what happened on the 1st of June. This document speaks about what the Sarajevo Romanija Corps did, we see it here, from the 22nd of May onwards. Do you recall that at the time, it had been agreed to exclude the use of fire-arms from 12.7-millimetre calibre onwards?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. I have never seen it before, and this doesn't really ring any bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at the time, there was a cease-fire that was on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I do not want to be sarcastic, but there has been a lot of cease-fires and it could be -- it could well be that there was a cease-fire on that day, but I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Serb side -- well, I think that this is the time when weaponry was being monitored by the UN. Do you remember that it was forbidden to use all artillery pieces from 12.7-millimetre calibre upwards?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Artillery pieces were placed at that time. I don't recall that. If I remember correctly, it's this time where we talked about the demilitarisation of the Gorazde and Zepa enclaves, but I don't remember that at that time artillery pieces of calibre higher than 12.7 were actually monitored. I think that it post-dates that period, because we do not have the ways and means to monitor those artillery pieces at that time. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you doubt the authenticity of this document, this order of General Galic's to involve officers and even the police, if necessary, in order to rule out any possibility of firing at town using 12.7-millimetre-calibre weapons and bigger than that?
