You did see quite a few of Galic's documents, so do you know -- I mean, do you doubt the authenticity of this document? It's the OTP that provided this document to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not for the witness to speculate or give opinion about something, including the authenticity of a document he knows nothing about. In the meantime, I think deleting the last sentence of the witness's previous answer -- Ms. Edgerton, was that the reason?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, with respect to Your Honours, whether or not the document was provided by the OTP is no indication of the authenticity of the document, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he understands it by now. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we'll not admit this, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to put a few things to you in relation to which we have authentic documents; namely, that before the 1st of June, there was a cease-fire in force, the Serb side observed it within the scope of its possibilities, and it really went far, and, on the other hand, the Muslim side violated that cease-fire agreement. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, there have been so many cease-fires that I don't really remember them. I know that when there was a cease-fire, it didn't last for very long, and one party or the other would violate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in this case we have documents showing that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is reporting to the Main Staff about the situation as it was, and they cannot lie in such documents, they have to tell the truth. It never happened that they would lie in their reports. We have this document, if it's still here. I hope that you have it on the ELMO. That you have the translation on the ELMO, that is. You see, paragraph 1, all the things that the enemy was doing; attacking Faletic, Sucura Kuce -- can we have the next page in English, please? If you can stop at this point, yes. See, the enemy was also firing from Hotonj, and so on and so forth, at Vogosca as well. Can we have the next page, please. Paragraph 2, the next page. See, it says -- well, it says "number 1," but it's actually number 2. It says: "Our units have taken measures to observe the cease-fire." Can we move on to paragraph 6 now, please, the last sentence. Paragraph 6, here it is. Well, it says "number 5" here: [In English] "The problem of food, ammunition ... is really critical." [Interpretation] Now, number 8, the conclusion. Here is the conclusion: "The units of the corps, as a whole, are fully observing the order on the cessation of hostilities, but it is not being observed by the enemy at the entire front, and the most frequent fire is coming from the Muslim part of Sarajevo, Pazarici, Visoko, and from Igman. This is particularly strong when important delegations of VIPs come to Sarajevo. Since they only go to the Muslim side, they get a false picture of who it is that is not observing the signed cease-fire agreements." This is a strictly-confidential document, a military secret. It is not intended for the media. He is reporting to his superior command about the situation in the corps, and so on. Do you believe this, sir?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: There's nothing that shows me that this was something which actually happened. So there might have been provocations on the Bosnian side, yes, certainly, but to determine whether the situation of the Serb forces is as it was described here, I cannot know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the following correspond to your own experience; namely, that the Muslim forces would open fire when various delegations were there in order to tarnish the reputation of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. Karadzic, the witness didn't know anything about the content of this document. We'll not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At one point, you said that the Serbs have 122- and 150-millimetre artillery, but that the Muslim side does not have 122 and over 150; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, yes, and from the reports we received inside the town. So inside the town, we did not find any such pieces of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the Muslim side the one that reported to you about this or did it come from an impartial source?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I remind you of the fact that UNPROFOR was quite numerous in Sarajevo, we had observers, and these were the people who gave information to us on the presence or non-presence of heavy weaponry inside the town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D1943, please, could we have that document now. There's a translation there as well. Actually, I'm not sure that there is a translation. It's possible, though. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see, Witness, that under number D -- or, rather, subparagraph D, it says: "Howitzer battery, 122-millimetre D-30 with all personnel and materiel disposed in the 2nd Motorised Brigade." Do you know where the 2nd Motorised Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see here that they do have a 122-millimetre Howitzer? And here, under B, it says that they have 105-millimetre and also a 120-millimetre mortar battery. And I believe that you do know, on the whole, who the commander of the corps was and that you're familiar with the signature and everything else; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But as far as I know, the 1st Corps was not just for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the 1st Corps was in Sarajevo, but it had two divisions. Two were around Sarajevo and one was in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: When I was in Sarajevo, there were no divisions of the 1st Corps. There were only brigades of the Bosnian Muslim corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is correct. However -- that is correct. However, 10 or 12 brigades were within the town, itself; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185
utterances.text: Those are not the figures I tend to remember. For me, there were about eight brigades in town, if I remember correctly, but I might be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, because it shows that they did have 122-millimetre Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it shows or not, Ms. Edgerton, do you object to this admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, yes, for the same reasons as the documents previously. The witness has had absolutely nothing to offer on this document and, in fact, specifically denied some of the propositions put to him by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may I say something before you rule? Can I say something before you make your decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document denies the witness's denial. The witness may be denying something, but this document shows that the denial is not correct. The witness, their witness, cannot be aware of all of my documents, but can be aware of a particular phenomenon. This document directly contradicts what it was that the witness was claiming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can tender that document through another witness and challenge the credibility of this witness later on. We'll not admit it. Due to the meeting I have to attend at 3.30, officially, we should stop at 3.30, although the courtroom would be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we better adjourn now for today. And before we break, I have a question for Mr. Robinson, because I understand that all matters relating to binding orders is under your purview. What I'd like to know is whether you have any position about the Bosnian government correspondence filed on the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would like to have you invite them to an oral hearing, as you had for the other states, and we believe that there are a number of documents that have to be in their possession that are not being produced, and that the best way to resolve that is to invite them for an oral hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are minded to file something in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think we already filed something in writing, a supplemental submission which was suggested in oral hearing. I think we filed that in March sometime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you have nothing further except for the statement you just made?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll be resuming tomorrow at 2.15. In the meantime, Mr. Witness, if I can advise you not to discuss your evidence with anybody. Of course, you are free to speak to somebody, but you are not supposed to discuss your evidence. I hope you understood that. 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.
